turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I'll get your observations done before the doctor comes in. Sleeve up for me, please.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Of course, Sister. Thank you.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He's been quiet in the bakkie, but he walked in from the parking without any fuss.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I am quite well, thank you. We are only here for a check-up.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Hold still. I got one-fifty-six over ninety-eight, no, the cuff had slipped. It's one hundred and forty-eight over ninety-two.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that a concern, Sister?
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): The doctor will go through it with you. Pulse is seventy-eight, oxygen is ninety-seven percent, and your temperature is thirty-six point six.
[SEG0008] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He had a cup of rooibos just now, if that makes a difference.
[SEG0009] person_1 (NURSE): It doesn't. Any pain while you're sitting here?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Sister. Nothing at present.
[SEG0011] person_1 (NURSE): All right. He won't be long.
[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): Morning. Doctor Naidoo. What brings you in?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, Doctor. I have come for a check-up. I am sixty-two, my GP in Pietermaritzburg is away, and it seemed sensible not to wait.
[SEG0014] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I booked it. I didn't want this left for another month while his GP is off.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any complaints?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that I wish to trouble you with, Doctor. Um, I have been managing at the flat.
[SEG0017] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He needs to tell you about the stairs. He gets a tight feeling in his chest when he climbs them.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): I would not call it a complaint, exactly. I came to be looked over, that is all.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Doctor. I do not have chest pain.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Breathless?
[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He gets breathless on the hill by the shops. I've watched him stop halfway up.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): I would not say breathless, if I may. I slow my pace. It is not the same thing.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): How long has this stair business been going on?
[SEG0025] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The tight chest? Two weeks. It started just after the long weekend, I'm sure of it.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Forgive me, it is longer than that. About a month, perhaps a little more. I simply did not mention it at home.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): So which is it, two weeks or a month?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I cannot give you an exact day, Doctor. I am sorry. It came on gradually.
[SEG0029] person_3 (CAREGIVER): His brother's braai was two weeks back and he struggled on the stoep stairs that afternoon. That's when I first saw it.
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. What do you actually feel?

[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Well... a tight feeling across the chest, not a pain, and it came on gradually. It comes if I climb the stairs or if I walk fast to the robot, and if I stop it eases off. It has been about a month.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): Down the arm? Into the jaw?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No. It stays in the chest.
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): Nausea? Sweating?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): No nausea, Doctor. And I do not sweat with it.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): At rest? At night?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Only with the effort.
[SEG0038] person_4 (DOCTOR): Cough?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough.
[SEG0040] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any illnesses I should know about?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): High blood pressure. I have had it for five-ish years.
[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): So, known high blood pressure. Tablets?
[SEG0043] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He takes a blood pressure tablet every morning for his pressure. It's amlodipine, five milligrams. I pop it out of the blister for him.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): I must disagree, I am afraid. The strength is ten milligrams. I am quite sure of the current bottle.
[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): Five or ten?
[SEG0046] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The blister pack at the flat says five. I looked this morning.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): And the chemist dispensed ten milligrams when I collected it. We shall have to compare the boxes, I suppose.
[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): Bring the box next visit. I won't guess the strength. Every day, though?
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, Doctor. Every morning, without fail. It is for the blood pressure.
[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): Anything else?

[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Aspirin, by mouth, seventy-five milligrams... no, forgive me, that was the old dose, it is a hundred and fifty milligrams. My GP said once a day, for the heart, as a precaution. I take it on and off, I am sorry to say.
[SEG0052] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Some weeks it's three days, some weeks four. He leaves it on the saucer.
[SEG0053] person_4 (DOCTOR): So not as prescribed.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): That is correct. I cannot pretend otherwise.
[SEG0055] person_4 (DOCTOR): Allergies?
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): None, Doctor. I have no allergies.
[SEG0057] person_3 (CAREGIVER): You told me you got a rash from penicillin when you were younger. You won't touch the stuff.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): That was an upset stomach, not a rash, and I do not count it as an allergy.
[SEG0059] person_4 (DOCTOR): You're not agreed, then. Any operations?
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Doctor. I have never had an operation.
[SEG0061] person_4 (DOCTOR): Heart disease in the family?
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): My father had a heart attack in his seventies.
[SEG0063] person_4 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): I stopped, about ten years ago. I hardly drink, a glass of wine at Christmas and nothing more.
[SEG0065] person_4 (DOCTOR): And day to day, work, home?

[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): I am retired. I was an accounts clerk at the municipality. Mrs Khumalo lives in as my carer, and the flat is on the third floor, which is rather the trouble with the stairs.
[SEG0067] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The lift is out half the time with load shedding, but that's a whole other story.
[SEG0068] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll listen to your chest. Deep breaths.
[SEG0069] person_4 (DOCTOR): Chest is clear. Heart sounds are normal, no murmur. Pulses are present. No swelling at the ankles.
[SEG0070] person_2 (PATIENT): I am glad to hear that.
[SEG0071] person_4 (DOCTOR): This tightness on effort could be angina. I can't confirm it today.
[SEG0072] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Should he stop walking to the shops?
[SEG0073] person_4 (DOCTOR): No. Walk, but don't rush. If the tightness comes, stop and rest. If it starts at rest, or it goes on more than a few minutes, go to casualty.
[SEG0074] person_4 (DOCTOR): Take the aspirin every day, a hundred and fifty milligrams, no skipping. Keep taking the blood pressure tablet each morning until we've seen the box.

[SEG0075] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand, Doctor. I shall walk without rushing, rest if it tightens, and go to casualty should it start at rest or carry on. I shall take the aspirin every day, and I shall keep on with the morning blood pressure tablet.
[SEG0076] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll do an ECG today, and bloods for cholesterol and glucose.
[SEG0077] person_1 (NURSE): I can do the ECG and the bloods in the side room once you're done.
[SEG0078] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good. Come back next week for the results. Reception will book it.
[SEG0079] person_2 (PATIENT): Next week will suit me well, and I shall bring the tablet box. Thank you kindly.
[SEG0080] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll make sure the box comes with us, Doctor.
[SEG0081] person_1 (NURSE): Whenever you're ready, sir.

clinical_actions.description: Electrocardiogram

clinical_uncertainties.description: The caregiver says the chest tightness has lasted two weeks, while the patient says about a month, and this was not settled.
The patient cannot give an exact day when the chest tightness began.
The caregiver reports breathlessness on the hill, but the patient denies being breathless.
The caregiver says amlodipine is 5 mg and the patient says it is 10 mg, and the doctor would not choose a strength.
Aspirin was prescribed once daily, but the patient takes it only on and off, some weeks about three days and some weeks four, rather than every day.
The patient denies any allergy, while the caregiver recalls a penicillin rash that the patient says was only an upset stomach.

spec.situation: Man or woman 50-70 who comes 'for a check-up' and only slowly admits a tight feeling in the chest when climbing stairs or walking fast; first denies chest pain, later describes the tightness. Takes a BP tablet and aspirin on and off. Doctor orders ECG and bloods.
features: relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.

omissions.text: Patient denied chest pain when specifically asked.
Aspirin adherence detail: patient takes it only on and off, some weeks about 3 to 4 days rather than daily as prescribed.
